Chapter 2: The Temptation to Escape and the Limits of Reason.
When you finally see just how absurd life can be, it’s totally normal to want to escape it.
People have always tried to make sense of things—to find patterns, explanations, anything that brings a little comfort. Some turn to philosophy, hoping reason and logic will somehow unlock the answers. Others put their faith in something higher, trusting that there’s a purpose behind all the chaos.
Picture this: someone sitting alone late at night, surrounded by stacks of books and scribbled notes, desperately trying to piece together the puzzle of existence. They pore over the words of great thinkers, searching for some master plan that makes it all fit. But the thing is, the deeper they dig, the more they realize—every answer just leads to more questions.
The world stays stubbornly silent, never really giving up its secrets.
Philosophers have tried to build these grand theories to explain everything, but, in the end, those systems always lean on assumptions that can’t actually be proven. Sure, it’s comforting for a while, but it quietly asks you to have faith in something you can’t really see.
Reason can only take you so far. The absurd is always there, lurking just outside every explanation.
When reason hits its walls, some people turn to religion. They find comfort in believing a higher power is guiding things, that suffering matters, that there’s life after this one. It can bring real peace—no doubt about it—but it also takes a leap of faith. You have to accept things you can’t see or prove.
Imagine a grieving parent, holding onto the hope that they’ll see their child again in another world. That hope makes the pain bearable, but it’s also a way of turning away from the absurd—escaping the question instead of answering it.
And there are even subtler escapes. Some throw themselves into work, thinking achievement will give life meaning. Others chase pleasure, hoping happiness will fill the emptiness. But those distractions don’t last. Sooner or later, that nagging question creeps back in—usually in the quiet moments, when there’s nothing left to distract the mind.
Wanting to escape the absurd makes sense. Nobody likes living with uncertainty and doubt. But every escape comes with a price. It means giving up the chance to live honestly—to face life exactly as it is. It’s about accepting someone else’s answers instead of searching for your own.
But here’s something important: there’s a kind of freedom in refusing to escape. It’s the freedom to live without illusions, to take the world as it really is. That doesn’t mean giving up on hope or joy. It just means letting go of the need for certainty.
It’s about learning to live with questions that might never have answers.
Most people never reach this place. The comfort of escape is just too tempting, and the fear of the unknown is too real.
But for those who are willing to face the absurd head-on, there’s a different kind of peace—a peace that comes from living authentically, without pretending the world is something it’s not.
